Trump’s Iran Deal: Oil Now, Nukes Later

The Trump administration just handed Iran the one thing sanctions were supposed to choke forever: the ability to sell oil at full market price again, even as the nuclear file stays deliberately murky. 

For 60 days, Treasury has lifted key oil sanctions, letting Tehran pump, ship and charge real prices instead of begging buyers to risk U.S. penalties for a discount. The war isn’t over, but the cash register is back on.

JD Vance came out of day one in Switzerland claiming a win: he says Iran agreed to invite U.N. nuclear inspectors back into its facilities, promising “Major Weapons Inspections” in Trump’s trademark caps. 

Tehran’s version? “No new commitments.” Iran’s foreign ministry insists any IAEA access will happen only “under existing procedures,” which could mean the limited, half‑blind inspections that survived after Trump shredded the 2015 deal and after U.S. and Israeli strikes drove inspectors out last year. 

The IAEA itself hasn’t rushed to back Vance’s narrative.

The whole thing looks like a badly dubbed replay of the Obama‑era accord Trump called “one of the Worst Deals ever,” right down to the inspectors and sanctions relief — only this time Tehran is sitting across from a man who already tore up one agreement and then bombed its capital. 

Iran keeps saying its program is civilian, swears it won’t build a bomb, and vows it will “never back down” from its right to enrich uranium. The hardest questions about how much enriched stockpile stays, where, and under what inspection regime are politely kicked to “later.”

On the ground, the cease-fire architecture is being held together with duct tape and Qatar Airways mileage. Vance and Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrapped a marathon session mediated by Qatari and Pakistani officials with talk of “encouraging progress” and new hotlines for the Strait of Hormuz and Lebanon. 

Traffic through Hormuz has picked up but remains well below prewar levels, trapped between Vance insisting “the strait is open” and Iran periodically threatening — and sometimes claiming — to close it whenever Israel and Hezbollah trade fire.

Meanwhile, the money question hovers. Vance floated a framework to unfreeze Iranian assets “at a later date,” while Iran’s central bank hints that “necessary memoranda were signed” to start the process. 

That ambiguity is the deal in miniature: enough relief to get oil flowing and inflation down before a U.S. election, enough vagueness that both sides can pretend they didn’t blink on nukes. 

The war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes in February is now being paused on a 60‑day license and a promise to talk about uranium later. It’s less a grand bargain than a breathing tube — for markets, for Trump, and for a regime that has learned exactly how much pain Washington is willing to take before it starts paying for “peace” it once swore it would never buy.
